background.speaker: [target]
background.text: Thank you, Rahul, and delighted to be here at the India Today Conclave. I think one of the most prestigious and outstanding events which India Today manages to do year after year.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_02
background.text: We are delighted to have you here, sir. Shaun, of all political and economic rhetoric, bankers are often the best people to get a strong financial sense of the state of the Indian economy. We're seeing some macro green shoots in terms of India being amongst the fastest growing global economies. Private investment, though, is refusing to kick off. We were here a couple of years ago on the back of corporate taxes coming down, and you'd expressed hope that this would create a virtuous investment cycle. We're still waiting for that cycle to kickstart. And we're seeing household savings, which had been one of the big strength areas of the Indian economy, now declining, as is the case in many countries. So could you start by giving us a temperature reading of your understanding of the current growth prospects and the state of the Indian economy?

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: I think in the last three years, in the post-COVID period, India has come out remarkably better than what I would have thought about at the beginning of COVID, which is March 20. And if you look at three years later, we look like in a much better place than what we would have thought. Therefore, India has battered and navigated through the COVID period extremely well. Simultaneously, if you look at the Russia-Ukraine situation, India has once again positioned itself so beautifully from a geopolitical point of view, and actually Indian economics getting lower energy for India, at the same time standing up in the world to say, India will think for its own interests versus anything else. These two are one of the most outstanding developments from an economic point of view in a fast-changing geopolitical landscape. And kudos to all of us. In this... In this country, and particularly to all the policymakers and the government for really bringing us and navigating us through what was clearly three years of turbulence. And therefore, I do believe from a temperature check point of view, India is in a good place. However, the world is not in such a good place. And the reason I say it is because the U.S. has lived off the world's money for a long time. Because most of the countries around the world keep their surpluses with the U.S. And therefore, U.S. gets all the money being the reserve currency. And at the same time, U.S. deficits are very high. And you've seen from zero interest rates, interest rates now in U.S. have moved up more than 500 basis points and don't seem to be stopping. And the world's reserve currency, if it pays 5.5% on its money, overnight, then the rest of the world has to adjust on the interest rates. So that is one part. Second is China. I frankly cannot figure out what is really happening inside China. And the latest Evergrande situation, which is a large real estate developer in China, has gone bust. They did not take quick action. It was a problem two years ago. Let it fester for a long time. And the Chinese economy is not in a shape which I think it should be for getting the world out of trouble. And then, of course, you have Russia, all the other issues. Therefore, the world, both economically and geopolitically, is not in a good place. Therefore, India is in a good place, but we are in an interdependent world.

And what do we need to do to change the rules of the game? Yes, we want to minimize accidents on the road. The way to do it is to have better traffic signals, better supervision, better regulation.
